summary: Specifies a per-domain technique for establishing inter-domain TE label switched paths, where each domain computes its own part of the path. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Each region plans its own part of a long trip, and they are linked to make the whole route.

questions: what is an inter-domain te lsp
what is ero expansion in rsvp-te
subtitle: Let each domain work out its own stretch of a long MPLS or GMPLS path as the signal moves along.

tldr.problem: The head-end router of a traffic engineering path often cannot see a complete path across several areas or autonomous systems, so it cannot compute the whole route itself.
tldr.mechanism: The signaling message names the destination and the next boundary routers. Each boundary router computes the path through its own domain and passes the setup on, using crankback to try another exit when a domain fails.
tldr.outcome: Inter-domain TE LSPs can be set up without sharing topology between domains, but the result is not guaranteed to be optimal or to allow diverse paths.

today: RFC 5152 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Per-Domain Computation
sections.content:
A domain here is a group of network elements under common address management or path computation responsibility, such as an IGP area or an Autonomous System. When the head-end LSR cannot see a complete end-to-end path across domains, this RFC describes computing the path domain by domain while the LSP is being set up.

The RFC focuses only on path computation. Requirements come from RFC 4105 and RFC 4216, the framework from RFC 4726, and signaling from RFC 5151 and RFC 5150. The RFC admits this is one technique among many, and that a Path Computation Element approach (RFC 4655) could be better if an end-to-end constrained shortest path is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: When no one router can see the whole map, each region plans its own part of the route.

sections.title: Assumptions and Topologies
sections.content:
Every domain is assumed to run traffic engineering (OSPF-TE or ISIS-TE and RSVP-TE), and LSPs are signaled with RSVP-TE (RFC 3209, RFC 3473). The path in the ERO may mix strict and loose hops, such as the complete path in the source domain followed by boundary LSRs or AS numbers. Boundary LSRs must be able to expand loose hops locally. No topology or resource information needs to be distributed between domains, which preserves scalability and confidentiality.

Constraints such as bandwidth can be used across domains, but others, like resource affinity and color, may need translating at domain borders using a local mapping based on policy. The RFC uses two example networks: an inter-area case with ABR1 to ABR4, and an inter-AS case with three ASs joined by ASBRs.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone knows their own neighborhood, but no maps are swapped between neighborhoods. At the borders, they agree on how to translate each other's rules.

sections.title: How Each Boundary Router Computes
sections.content:
A boundary LSR that gets a Path message with a loose hop follows RFC 5151 and then these steps. If the next hop is not in its TED, it checks that the hop is outside the domain and that the next domain is Packet Switch Capable with an in-band control channel. It then SHOULD check IP reachability through the IGP or BGP. This is the optional auto-discovery of the exit point. If the next hop is unreachable, it SHOULD send a PathErr with error code 24 (Routing Problem).

For a contiguous TE LSP, the boundary LSR SHOULD perform an ERO expansion: compute the constrained path to the next loose hop and add it as strict hops. For a stitched or nested LSP, it SHOULD use or signal an intra-domain H-LSP or S-LSP to the next boundary LSR, if local policy allows. If neither works, a PathErr is sent upstream.

If a downstream boundary router fails to find a path, the upstream one can try another exit boundary LSR when crankback (RFC 4920) is allowed. If it is not allowed, the boundary LSR MUST stop and forward the PathErr toward the head-end.
sections.plainLanguage: At each border, the guard works out the way across their own land and passes the trip along. If the road ahead is blocked, they try another border crossing or tell the traveler.

sections.title: Inter-Area and Inter-AS Examples
sections.content:
In the inter-area case, R0 in area 1 sets up T0 to R1 in area 2. The path can be a set of loose hops such as R0-ABR1(loose)-ABR3(loose)-R1(loose), or a mix of strict and loose hops. R0 computes the path to ABR1, ABR1 picks the next ABR across area 0, and so on. If ABR3 fails, ABR1 can try ABR4 when crankback is allowed.

The inter-AS case is very similar, with T1 running from R0 in AS1 to R6 in AS3 and an extra complication: the links between ASBRs. As an optimization, ASBRs may flood TE information for the inter-ASBR links in their own IGP, without any IGP adjacency across them and without using them in SPF computations. This lets earlier routers pick a better route to the entry ASBR and potentially saves one level of crankback. No summarized TE information is leaked between ASs.

If setup fails, the head-end may select another sequence of loose hops, retry the same path, or retry after relaxing some constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples walk a trip across areas and across networks. In both, each border hands the trip on to the next, and a failed attempt can go back and try a different border.

sections.title: Path Optimality and Diversity
sections.content:
Because computation is per-domain, the RFC says one cannot guarantee that the optimal inter-domain path is found. Computing two diverse paths can also fail because of the well-known trapping problem. In its example topology, a first path A-B-C-D leaves no diverse partner, even though A-C-D and A-B-D would have been two diverse paths.

The service provider can choose the path computation method per LSP. If per-domain computation does not meet the requirements, other techniques such as PCE-based computation may be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Planning one piece at a time can lead you down a road that blocks a good second route, even if two good routes existed all along.

sections.title: Reoptimization
sections.content:
Reoptimizing an established inter-domain LSP is a requirement of RFC 4216 and RFC 4105. For a contiguous LSP, RFC 4736 lets the head-end learn of a better path downstream, and the head-end triggers Make-Before-Break as in RFC 3209.

For stitched or nested LSPs, reoptimization is a local matter in each domain, done by reoptimizing the intra-domain H-LSP or S-LSP. No extra RSVP signaling is needed and the head-end does not see it. An operator can still trigger it manually at the head-end. Procedures from RFC 4736 MUST be used if the operator does not want local reoptimization of certain LSPs, in which case events within the domain MUST be reported to the head-end.
sections.plainLanguage: If a shorter road opens up later, the trip can switch to it without stopping traffic. Each region can do that itself, or the starting point can ask for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Inter-domain signaling raises the security issues discussed in RFC 5151, and RFC 4726 summarizes the requirements. Operators may use RSVP-TE security features, which may need key sharing between domains (RFC 2747, RFC 3097) and frequent key changes. Operators SHOULD have policies and filters at domain borders, a way to rate-limit setup requests or error notifications, and policy-based outbound RSVP message processing.

This method adds no information exchanged between ASs and preserves topology confidentiality. Boundary nodes that compute paths may be exposed to attacks, so supporting policy decisions to reject ERO expansion is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Borders should check who is asking, slow down anyone asking too much, and be allowed to say no to a request.
